metadata.label: Pub Note
metadata.value: This 1939 map of Antarctica was produced by the Property and Survey Branch of the Australian Department of the Interior in Canberra, compiled, drawn, and lithographed by E. P. Bayliss, F.R.G.S. It was prepared jointly with the Department of External Affairs and accompanied by a Handbook and Index to accompany a Map of Antarctica, written by Bayliss and J. S. Cumpston. The map documented contemporary geographic knowledge and the territorial claims established in the Antarctic during the preceding decades, particularly the Australian Antarctic Territory, transferred to Australian authority by British Order in Council in 1933 and accepted by Australian legislation that year. The principal map uses an azimuthal equidistant projection centered on the South Pole, with a stated latitudinal scale of 1:10,000,000. It delineates the Australian Antarctic Territory, including Enderby, Kemp, Mac-Robertson, Princess Elizabeth, Kaiser Wilhelm II, Queen Mary, Wilkes, King George V, and Oates Lands, as well as the Falkland Islands Dependency, Ross Dependency, and French Adélie Land. Red lines identify territorial boundaries and subdivisions. Coastal annotations identify explorers and discovery dates, while bathymetric contours, soundings, glaciers, and elevations record the uneven state of exploration. A table identifies the legal instruments creating the principal dependencies. The map also incorporates recent discoveries, including observations associated with the German Antarctic expedition of 1938–1939 and the Norwegian claim to Queen Maud Land in January 1939. Two inset maps provide additional geographic context. A long inset across the upper margin, Coastal Regions of the Australian Antarctic Territory, depicts the Australian sector at 1:7,000,000. Another, The Antarctic Continent in Relation to the Principal Land Masses in the Southern Hemisphere, places Antarctica in relation to Australia, New Zealand, and South America at 1:60,000,000. The compilation followed extensive research begun in 1938 by Bayliss and Cumpston, who reportedly examined approximately 250 sources, including expedition reports, maps, charts, and government documents. Earlier departmental compilations had become outdated as aerial and maritime exploration expanded knowledge of the continent. The finished map was printed by L. F. Johnston, Commonwealth Government Printer, Canberra. It was sold in a single-sheet version, accompanied by the handbook, and in a larger two-sheet version. Its comprehensive synthesis of geographic discoveries, hydrographic information, and competing territorial jurisdictions makes it an important document of Antarctic mapping immediately before the Second World War. (Ruderman, 2026)

metadata.label: Pub Note
metadata.value: Atlante geografico polare by Silvio Zavatti. Published by Poligrafiche Bolis in Forlì, Italy, in 1958. Bound in board with a blue linen spine. Front cover features a map of Antarctica and an illustration of polar bears. Title translates to: Polar geographic atlas. Volume includes a title page, table of contents, dedication, preface, general text and individual descriptions of each map, as well as 43 maps on 15 plates. The maps represent the Arctic, Greenland and Antarctica, including islands in both the Arctic and Antarctic Regions. The final four maps each depict a quadrant of Antarctica. Maps show political boundaries, cities, topography, mountain peaks, bodies of water, drainage, coastlines, islands and water depths. The work stands out for its scientific accuracy and the richness of its cartographic information, making it a key reference for scholars and enthusiasts of polar geography. Zavatti, a renowned explorer and scholar of polar territories, devoted much of his life to the research and documentation of these remote areas. Throughout his career, Zavatti led numerous expeditions to Greenland and Antarctica, significantly contributing to our understanding of the Arctic and Antarctica. Today, the Silvio Zavatti Polar Geographic Institute in Fermo, Italy, preserves his extensive body of research, continuing to serve as a key center for polar geographic studies.

metadata.label: Pub Reference
metadata.value: Chart appeared in "The Siege of the South Pole, the Story of Antarctic Exploration by Hugh Robert Mill, LL.D., D.Sc. With Maps, Diagrams, and Other Illustrations and Maps by J.G. Bartholomew [with:] Chart of the South Polar Regions"

metadata.label: Pub Note
metadata.value: "This 1905 chart of the South Pole by cartographer J. G. Bartholomew offers a comprehensive depiction of Antarctica and its exploration history up to the early 20th century, integrating data from multiple expeditions and showcasing both known and unexplored territories. At the turn of the 20th century, Antarctica remained largely a mystery, with vast areas uncharted and unexplored. This chart, compiled from the latest sources available in 1905, represents a significant effort to consolidate existing knowledge about the South Pole. Its delineation of unexplored regions in white, open sea in dark blue, and known land alongside explorers' routes, provides a visual narrative of the human endeavor to understand this remotest part of the world. It documents key explorations, including those of Weddell in 1833, and presents ocean soundings, revealing both the depth of human knowledge and the vastness of the unknown. The chart includes an inset of the British Isles, shown to scale, highlighting the geographical and conceptual distance between the familiar and the frontier of exploration. Additionally, the left edge of the sheet features a series of maps of Antarctica from 1760 to 1905, portraying the evolving understanding of the region. These maps color-code land, sea, and unexplored areas, with the black representing unexplored territory progressively shrinking over time, visually encapsulating the progress of exploration. The historical significance of the Chart of the South Polar Regions lies in its encapsulation of a romantic era of exploration. It chronicles the progression from Cook's voyages in the 1770s to the expeditions of Gerlache, Scott, Bruce, Drygalski, and Nordenskiold in the early 20th century. The chart is a fantastic and attractive summary of the state of knowledge before the final push for the South Pole in the following years." (Ruderman, 2025)

metadata.label: Pub Note
metadata.value: Hand colored map of the southern Polar Region (Antarctic) , 20x23, based upon the map of Philippe Bauche, published in Paris. This map in black and white, drawn by the scientific geographer M. Buache was published in 1763 by the Gentleman's Magazine, a famous 18th century English journal, as part of an article entitled Geographical and Physical Observations, A new theory of the earth, including a Theory of the Antarctic Regions, and the frozen Sea which they are supposed to contain, according to the Hypothesis of the M. Buache. This chart centers on the South Pole and extends northwards as far as the Tropic of Capricorn. Though predating the discovery of Antarctica by more than half a century, Buache's map details a fanciful Antarctic Pole sandwiched between the tip of Cape Horn, the Cape of Good Hope, and southern Australia, which stretches northwards off the map as far as New Guinea to which the mainland of Australia erroneously attached and Indonesia in the upper left. The map also showing 17th & 18th century land and ice sightings in the southern seas, and name drops De L'Isle, Drake, Halley, and even Ortelius. Heading inward towards the Pole, the map shows a circle labeled ‘Land Yet Undiscovered,' and another within that, labeled ‘Frozen Sea as Supposed.' None of which stops it from depicting the best guesses as to what might exist there. Most interestingly, New Zealand is only the northernmost tip of a great southern continent. Buache was an academic geographer who researched his material thoroughly, relying on the most up-to-date information from voyages of discovery.

metadata.label: Pub Note
metadata.value: Ruscelli's Italian translation from the Greek of Ptolemy's Geographia. The fourth edition of Ruscelli's Ptolemy, revised, enlarged, and edited by Giuseppe Rosaccio, 4 parts in one volume, with 69 engraved double-page uncolored maps, five entirely new maps, including one of the Americas. With various pagination, showing landmarks, rivers, ports, fortifications, major cities and towns, some with decorative cartouches, illustrations of sea monsters and ships. Relief shown pictorially. Bound in full leather covers. Claudius Ptolemy (90-168 CE) was a Roman geographer and mathematician living in Egypt, who compiled his knowledge and theories about the world's geography into one seminal work. Although his maps did not survive, his mathematical projections and location coordinates did. Girolamo Ruscelli (c. 1504-1566) was a Venetian editor, whose maps are primarily based on those by Jacopo Gastaldi (1548) but with many of his own additions and reproduced on a larger scale. Ruscelli introduces several important innovations in this volume through his 37 "modern" maps, which cover Europe, Africa, Asia and the New World. Ruscelli includes a double hemisphere world map, which was the first of its kind to be used in an atlas, and "Carta Marina Nuova Tavola", a rare sea chart of the world.
